passage:
Akash, come sit, beta. I am Gurpreet, and I'll tell you something from when I was a boy of ten, in fourth standard. A flowerpot fell and broke in the verandah. Eight of us stood around the pieces, and back then I stood there shaking inside, because our teacher was already walking over.

Somebody whispered, “Bittu did it.” Bittu was the smallest, and he never argued. Everyone nodded so fast. I nodded too, and my shaking stopped. Bittu's ears went red, and he looked at the floor.

That night the sweeper told us the wind had knocked it over. I couldn't eat. Next morning I told Bittu I was sorry, and I told our teacher the truth.

qa.q: What did somebody whisper after the flowerpot broke?
qa.a: Somebody whispered, “Bittu did it,” and everyone nodded.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet's shaking stop when everyone nodded?
qa.a: Gurpreet was afraid of being blamed, and once the blame landed on Bittu the fear felt lifted. The relief was real, even if it was unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Gurpreet make the next morning after learning about the wind?
qa.a: Gurpreet told Bittu sorry and told the teacher the truth, rather than letting the blame stay on Bittu.

qa.q: What was it like for Bittu, standing there with red ears and looking at the floor?
qa.a: Bittu likely felt small, alone and ashamed, since everyone agreed against Bittu and Bittu never argued back.

grounding: An elder recalls how a group of children pinned a broken pot on the smallest child to calm their own fear, and how he later set it right.

passage:
Two minutes before the teacher came back, the class fish tank was overflowing onto the floor. Irawati's heart hammered. She had been the last one at the tap, and she knew it. Around her, seven children stared at the puddle.

“Santosh must have left the tap on,” Irawati said quickly. Nobody asked. Two others nodded. Someone said, “He's always fiddling.” Irawati felt her stomach loosen, like she had put a heavy bag down.

Santosh's eyes filled. He said nothing, just grabbed a rag and started wiping. Jaya stood by the tap, arms folded, and did not nod.

The relief lasted until the door opened. Irawati looked at Santosh's bent back, and her stomach tightened again.

qa.q: Who did Irawati say had left the tap on?
qa.a: Irawati said Santosh must have left the tap on.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's stomach loosen after the class agreed it was Santosh?
qa.a: Irawati was afraid of being blamed as the last one at the tap, and the blame moving to Santosh felt like putting a heavy bag down.

qa.q: What could Irawati try when the door opens and the teacher asks what happened?
qa.a: Irawati could admit to being the last at the tap and say the blame on Santosh was a guess.

qa.q: How does Jaya see the moment, standing by the tap with arms folded?
qa.a: Jaya seems to disagree with blaming Santosh and does not want to go along, but staying silent shows how hard it is to speak against the group.

grounding: When a fish tank overflows, a child pins the blame on one weaker child to calm the group's own fear of being blamed.

passage:
Wednesday night
Today the class plant pot broke during free period. Ma'am asked who did it. Everyone went quiet. Then Sunny said, “Kavitha was near the window.” And everyone said, “Yes, Kavitha!” I said it too.
Kavitha is new and very quiet. She just stood there with her mouth open. Ma'am made her stay back to clean.
The truth is Sunny's ball hit it. I saw. But when everyone said Kavitha, my tummy stopped feeling scared. Like it was over and nobody would ask me.
Now it's night and I feel weird. Kavitha didn't even cry. She just looked at the floor.
Tomorrow I will tell Ma'am what I saw.
Raghav

qa.q: What did Sunny say about Kavitha?
qa.a: Sunny said Kavitha was near the window.

qa.q: Why did Raghav's tummy stop feeling scared when everyone said Kavitha?
qa.a: Raghav felt relieved that the blame had landed on someone, so nobody would ask Raghav.

qa.q: Is Raghav's plan for tomorrow a good one, and why?
qa.a: Yes; telling Ma'am what he saw can clear Kavitha and stop one quiet child carrying the group's blame.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel after being blamed?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt, confused and alone, looking at the floor and cleaning up for something she didn't do.

grounding: A child writes about joining the class in blaming a quiet new girl for a broken pot, which calmed the writer's own fear of being blamed.

passage:
The bell rope at the village temple snapped while the children were swinging on it. Pujari ji came out, furious. “Who did this?”
The children looked at each other. Then Pappu pointed. “Lakshmi was pulling it!”
“Yes, Lakshmi!” said the others. Lakshmi was the smallest, the one who always came last in races.
Gautam had pulled hardest of all. He said nothing, and felt his shoulders loosen as Pujari ji turned to Lakshmi.
Lakshmi burst into tears. Pujari ji sent her home.
Gautam walked home slowly behind her. Her plaits bounced as she sobbed. That evening, he went back to the temple alone and told Pujari ji that he had pulled hardest. Pujari ji listened, sighed, and went to Lakshmi's house to apologise.

qa.q: Who pointed at Lakshmi first?
qa.a: Pappu pointed at her first.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when his shoulders loosened?
qa.a: He felt relieved that the blame had fallen on Lakshmi, not him, even though he had pulled hardest.

qa.q: What turned things around, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Gautam went back and told Pujari ji the truth, so Lakshmi was cleared and got an apology that same evening.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt being sent home?
qa.a: She was probably scared, humiliated and very alone, blamed because she was the smallest.

grounding: Shows village children pinning blame on the smallest child, which relieves their own fear, until one boy tells the truth.

passage:
In their classroom in Porto, the fish tank crashed to the floor during lunch break. Water everywhere, two goldfish flapping.
Mrs Silva rushed in. “What happened?”
Tomás, who had been leaning on the tank, said quickly, “Jamal bumped it.”
“Yeah, Jamal,” said three voices. Jamal stood by the wall, his face red, trying to speak, stuck on the first word as he sometimes was.
Ines had seen everything. She had been laughing with Tomás right beside the tank. She heard herself say, “Jamal,” too, and felt her chest loosen.
Mrs Silva looked at each of them. “Who actually saw Jamal touch it?”
Silence. Ines looked at Jamal's face, then at the floor. “I didn't,” she whispered. “It was Tomás leaning.”

qa.q: What were the two goldfish doing on the floor?
qa.a: They were flapping.

qa.q: How did Ines feel when she said "Jamal" too?
qa.a: She felt relieved for a moment, her chest loosening, because the blame was going somewhere else.

qa.q: What did Mrs Silva's question do well?
qa.a: Asking who actually saw it made the children check facts instead of repeating the group's blame, which let Ines tell the truth.

qa.q: How might Jamal have felt standing by the wall?
qa.a: He likely felt frightened and trapped, blamed while struggling to get his first word out.

grounding: Shows children pinning blame on a weaker child to calm their own fear, until a teacher asks for evidence and one girl tells the truth.

passage:
The class globe lay on the floor with a crack across Africa when Mrs Dutta walked in. "Who did this?"
Silence. Then Rohan said, "Must be Joseph. He's always clumsy."
Swati felt the knot in her stomach loosen. She had bumped that table during the chase game, though she wasn't sure the globe fell then. "Yes, Joseph was near it," she said. Three more voices joined. "Joseph broke the duster last month."
Joseph, small and quiet on the last bench, shook his head and looked at his shoes.
Mrs Dutta looked around. "Who actually saw it fall?" No hands. "Then nobody knows. Joseph, you're not in trouble. We'll all talk about the chase game after lunch."
Swati stared at her desk, face burning.

qa.q: Where was the crack on the class globe?
qa.a: The globe had a crack across Africa.

qa.q: Why did Swati join in blaming Joseph?
qa.a: Swati was afraid of being blamed herself after bumping the table, and pointing at Joseph made that fear ease.

qa.q: What did Mrs Dutta's question "Who actually saw it fall?" achieve?
qa.a: It asked for facts instead of guesses, showed nobody knew, and protected Joseph from the group's blame.

qa.q: What was it like for Joseph when everyone named him?
qa.a: Joseph likely felt helpless and hurt, unable to argue with the whole class, so he just shook his head and looked down.

grounding: Shows children quickly agreeing that one quieter child broke something, which eases their own fear of being blamed.
